d: The finger of peritoneum that leads the testis through the inguinal canal as it descends. Its lower end becomes the tunica vaginalis. If it stays open, it allows a communicating hydrocele or an indirect hernia.
Abnormal germ cells still confined to the seminiferous tubules. It is the precursor of most testicular germ cell tumors in adults, including seminoma and embryonal carcinoma.

An unusually high attachment of the tunica vaginalis that leaves the testis hanging free, like the clapper inside a bell. The testis can then twist its spermatic cord. The defect is usually present on both sides.
Relief of scrotal pain when the testis is lifted. It favors epididymitis, because lifting eases the pull on the inflamed epididymis. The sign is absent in testicular torsion.
A glomerulus-like structure in which tumor cells wrap around a central blood vessel inside a small space. It is the histologic hallmark of yolk sac tumor.
Rod-shaped pink inclusions in the cytoplasm of Leydig cells. They help identify a Leydig cell tumor, which makes androgens or estrogens rather than AFP or hCG.

Lifting of the testis on the same side when the inner thigh is stroked (L1 to L2). The sensory limb runs in the ilioinguinal nerve and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve; the motor limb is the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. It is usually absent in torsion and present in epididymitis.
A normal testis that the cremaster muscle pulls out of the scrotum but that comes down easily and stays down. Unlike a truly undescended testis, it needs observation, not orchiopexy.
